purpose: Eleven initial regional finding-aid connections. These records do not promote profile research counts, imply Indigenous territorial boundaries, or count overlapping directory names as distinct nations.

associations.name: Munsee
associations.associationType: Present community government location; one Munsee access point
associations.evidenceNote: Munsee-Delaware Nation identifies itself as a Lunaape band government on the northern shore of the Thames River, southwest of London, Ontario. This provides a present Ontario route for the broader Munsee directory entry through one specific Lenape-related community.
associations.reviewedScope: Read About page's opening paragraph and Lenni Lenape history paragraphs; language section also inspected but not used for classification.
limits: The Munsee directory access point encompasses more than this one government. Do not merge Munsee-Delaware Nation with Stockbridge-Munsee Community, Eelūnaapèewii Lahkèewiit, or other Lenape governments.
No population, land-area, subgroup taxonomy, or language-family assertion is adopted from this page.

associations.name: Natchez
associations.period: Historical Natchez communities in southwest Mississippi; source updated 2024-08-16
associations.sourceTitle: The Natchez Indians — Natchez National Historical Park
associations.evidenceNote: The National Park Service explicitly situates Natchez ancestors and communities in southwest Mississippi, including the Grand Village and Emerald Mound area. This is a historical Mississippi connection, not a claim that contemporary Natchez people are confined to that state.
associations.reviewedScope: Read the complete short article. Geographic use is confined to the opening paragraph and named historical mound centers.
limits: Do not adopt the article's sweeping disappearance, near-annihilation, or undisputed-French-possession language as an account of Natchez identity or contemporary rights.
The source's broad archaeological chronology and ancestry narrative were not independently assessed for this map record.

associations.name: Natchitoches
associations.associationType: Historical people connection in a community-published history
associations.period: Historical communities in the present Natchitoches Parish area; undated document inspected 2026-10-21
associations.sourceTitle: History of the Natchitoches Tribe of Louisiana
associations.sourceAuthor: Chief Fred D. Simon (as printed on the document)
associations.evidenceNote: The community-published history places the Natchitoches people around Black Lake and the present Natchitoches Parish, in northwest-central Louisiana. Its initial discussion also distinguishes historical Caddo-related peoples and confederacies rather than treating every Caddo-related name as the same political body.
associations.reviewedScope: Inspected the seven-page PDF's title and historical-geography discussion on printed pages 1–2; also read the French-contact narrative on pages 3–4. The mapped claim uses only pages 1–2.
limits: The file URL contains a different middle initial; the printed author credit is Fred D. Simon.
Do not infer that the present Louisiana organization and Caddo Nation of Oklahoma are the same government.
No population extrapolations, recognition determination, language classification, or territorial extent is adopted.

associations.name: Nauset
associations.period: Colonial-era Nauset communities on Cape Cod; undated historical text hosted by the Town of Eastham
associations.sourceTitle: Nauset Indians — Town of Eastham, Massachusetts
associations.sourceType: Primary municipal public-history page reproducing an older account
associations.evidenceNote: Eastham's public-history page explicitly locates the historical Nauset people on Cape Cod in Massachusetts and identifies their principal village near present Eastham. This supports a historical Massachusetts route, rather than a connection inferred from Nauset place names alone.
associations.reviewedScope: Read all five substantive paragraphs. The opening geographic statement and village-location paragraph establish this finding aid.
limits: The page uses dated outsider terminology and old population/disappearance claims; none is adopted.
The Nauset access point is retained with historical scope. This does not settle their political relationship to Wampanoag communities or identify a present government.
The NPS whaling report was read selectively for context but is not the basis of this association; its broad Wampanoag framing does not resolve every Nauset naming question.

associations.name: Nêhiyaw
associations.associationType: Overlapping Cree/Plains Cree naming access point
associations.evidenceNote: Neal McLeod's article identifies nêhiyawak as the Plains Cree self-name and explicitly places Cree communities across Saskatchewan. The Nêhiyaw directory route therefore connects to Saskatchewan as an overlapping Cree/Plains Cree naming access point, without creating an additional distinct-nation count.
associations.reviewedScope: Read the complete article; mapped evidence comes from the opening naming/geography paragraph and the following discussion of regional dialect differences.
limits: The article prints the plural nêhiyawak; this map record does not claim to be a singular-form dictionary analysis.
Do not equate every regional Cree dialect, community, or government, or treat Plains Cree as the only Cree identity.
No current population, migration-date, ceremony, or treaty-rights conclusion is taken from this article.

associations.name: Neutral Nation
associations.period: Historical early-seventeenth-century communities; current museum interpretation inspected 2026-10-21
associations.sourceTitle: Sho’aríshon Park — Lincoln Museum & Cultural Centre
associations.evidenceNote: The museum identifies historical Neutral communities around Lincoln and the northern shores of Lakes Ontario and Erie; its public interpretation site is in Jordan, Ontario. It treats Neutral Nation, Attawandaron and Hatiwendaronk as historical naming forms while explicitly noting uncertainty about the people's own name.
associations.reviewedScope: Read the historical introduction, The Neutral Nation paragraphs, and Location section. The Town of Lincoln's 2026 research-collection announcement was also inspected through its full indexed text and explicitly confirms southern Ontario/Niagara.
limits: Historical groups are not equated with a single contemporary government; dispersal does not establish disappearance of descendants.
No exact archaeological or burial location is reproduced.
The modern park's Mohawk spelling, contemporary art, and ceremonies are not generalized as historical Neutral language or practices.
Direct fetch of the municipal announcement failed; the main museum interpretation page was accessible and read directly.

associations.name: Nottoway
associations.associationType: Present community government and historical regional connection
associations.period: Contemporary state community description with historical Virginia context, inspected 2026-10-21
associations.sourceTitle: Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia — Secretary of the Commonwealth
associations.evidenceNote: Virginia's community account identifies the Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia as descending from the larger historical Nottoway community and describes its community house and interpretive center in Capron, Virginia. This gives the broader Nottoway entry an initial Virginia route through a named present community.
associations.reviewedScope: Read the substantive historical/community paragraphs, especially the distinction between the larger historical community and present tribe and the Capron community-facility paragraph.
limits: This source concerns Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia. Do not merge it with the separate Cheroenhaka (Nottoway) government.
The entry is a broad directory access point; no boundary or exclusive historical-state range is asserted.
This geographic record is not an independent federal-recognition review.

associations.name: Nuu-chah-nulth
associations.period: Current council self-description and contact location, inspected 2026-10-21
associations.evidenceNote: The Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council describes its support for Nuu-chah-nulth First Nations and communities and publishes its office in Port Alberni, British Columbia. This establishes an institutional British Columbia route for the collective directory name.
associations.reviewedScope: Read the homepage's Vision and Mission, community-service descriptions, and council address. The mission explicitly speaks of First Nations in the plural.
limits: This initial connection is to the council's published location, not a mapped homeland, reserve extent, or statement that every Nuu-chah-nulth First Nation has one government.
The council and the peoples/constituent First Nations are not interchangeable.
No separate deep-profile source count is assigned to this homepage.

associations.name: Ocanxiu (Sutiaba)
associations.period: Geographic context in a public 2013 assessment note; population context derives from the 2005 census
associations.sourceTitle: Readiness Preparation Proposal Assessment Note: Republic of Nicaragua, REDD+ Readiness Preparation Support
associations.sourceType: Primary World Bank project assessment document
associations.evidenceNote: Paragraph 40 explicitly identifies 'Ocanxiu or Sutiaba' among Indigenous peoples of Nicaragua's Pacific region. It supplies both the paired-name identification and a country connection, without requiring an inference from the Sutiaba place name.
associations.reviewedScope: Read title page and Representation and Participation of Indigenous Peoples, paragraphs 40–42, PDF pages 19–20. The association relies on paragraph 40, not population totals or general project commitments.
limits: The public version filename indicates December 2013; no present demographic estimate is claimed.
This is a broad Nicaragua finding aid and does not map communal titles, municipal boundaries, or the full historical language range.
The Penn DIA map catalogue was inspected but its map image failed to load; it is not substituted for an inspected map or counted as another geographic source.

associations.name: Oconee
associations.period: Oconee Old Town section, A.D. 1680–1715; dissertation published 2007
associations.sourceTitle: An Analysis of Historic Creek and Seminole Settlement Patterns, Town Design, and Architecture: The Paynes Town Seminole Site (8AL366), a Case Study
associations.sourceType: Original university doctoral dissertation with a focused historical-geographic synthesis
associations.evidenceNote: Blakney-Bailey's Oconee Old Town section describes an Oconee Lower Creek community relocating into north-central Georgia around 1690. It identifies the archaeological site near Milledgeville, Georgia as the likely location of that settlement. The community-history discussion, rather than the modern river name alone, supports this route.
associations.reviewedScope: Read title/date, Chapter 3 introduction on printed page 42, and Oconee Old Town subsection on printed pages 51–52, including its discussion of archaeological uncertainty and earlier investigations.
limits: The proposed archaeological identification remains 'likely' in the dissertation and is not upgraded to certainty.
This concerns the historical Oconee Lower Creek town/community, not every similarly named Cherokee or coastal community.
No precise archaeological coordinates, present-government identification, or exclusive territory is asserted.

The archaeological society's historical compilation was also read but is replaced here by the more clearly attributed dissertation; the large Swanton PDF was not accessible and is not claimed as inspected.

associations.name: Ofo
associations.associationType: Specific ancestral people within a present shared government
associations.period: Current tribal self-description of historical succession and present Louisiana location, inspected 2026-10-21
associations.sourceTitle: Our Culture — Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana
associations.evidenceNote: The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe identifies itself as successor to historical Tunica, Biloxi, Ofo and Avoyel communities, and names Ofo among its present ancestral constituents. Its reservation is near Marksville in central Louisiana. This gives Ofo an explicitly scoped descendant-community connection to Louisiana through a shared government.
associations.reviewedScope: Read the complete short Our Culture article, especially the succession/constituent paragraphs and the present-reservation description.
limits: Ofo, Tunica, Biloxi, Avoyel and Choctaw identities are not treated as synonyms; a shared government is not proof that these historical peoples were identical.
This is a descendant connection, not a claim that Louisiana encompasses the entire historical Ofo homeland.
No demographic total, land-area figure, language-family classification, or disappearance claim is adopted.

exclusions.name: Natchez
exclusions.note: An unrelated Choctaw source in the older profile was not reused. Replaced by direct NPS Natchez historical geography; sweeping termination language in that article is excluded.

exclusions.name: Ofo
exclusions.note: An unrelated Iowa Tribe reference in the older profile was not reused. Direct Tunica-Biloxi constituent history provides the connection.

exclusions.name: Neutral Nation
exclusions.note: An unrelated museum address/catalogue cannot establish historical Neutral geography. Direct Lincoln Museum interpretation was read.

exclusions.name: Ocanxiu (Sutiaba)
exclusions.note: A prior workshop lead did not independently establish both the alias and country. Map catalogue tags and an unread image were not used as substitute evidence.

gaps: These are initial region routes, not full-profile updates or exhaustive distributions. Historical and present institutional connections are deliberately distinguished.
Munsee and Nêhiyaw overlap other directory naming access points; Nuu-chah-nulth is collective. None of these connections changes distinct-nation counts.
Historical outsider summaries for Natchez and Nauset require broader Indigenous-led historiography during their later deep-profile research; dated disappearance language is not retained.
Other regions, descendant communities and contemporary governments remain to be researched. No absence or exclusion inference should be drawn from one initial region per entry.
